items.lede: On August 24, Oriel Bachar filed a deposition notice (Dkt. 77) in Case No. 26-11217 before Judge Walrath. The filing arrives one day before Papaya's objection deadline to Skillz's Motion to Compel Production of Documents and Certain Deposition Witnesses (Dkt. 73, objections due August 26), and three days before the virtual discovery hearing (Dkt. 76, August 28, 10:00 a.m. ET, Courtroom 4).
items.body_md:
On August 24, Oriel Bachar filed a deposition notice (Dkt. 77) in Case No. 26-11217 before Judge Walrath. The filing arrives one day before Papaya's objection deadline to Skillz's Motion to Compel Production of Documents and Certain Deposition Witnesses (Dkt. 73, objections due August 26), and three days before the virtual discovery hearing (Dkt. 76, August 28, 10:00 a.m. ET, Courtroom 4). The notice is substantive in classification — it is the foreign representative's own deposition notice, filed in direct response to the discovery dispute Skillz forced to a head via Dkt. 73 — but its significance is bounded: it reflects Papaya's willingness to put a witness forward, which potentially narrows the factual dispute before the court on Thursday, but it does not resolve whether Skillz's broader document production demands will be satisfied.

The strategic read is that Papaya filed Dkt. 77 ahead of its written objection to blunt at least the deposition-witness prong of Skillz's motion to compel. Skillz's Dkt. 73 attacked on two fronts — document production deficiencies and the availability of deposition witnesses — and Papaya's deposition notice, filed before the objection deadline, signals a concession on the witness availability issue while leaving the document production fight open. If Papaya's August 26 objection confirms that posture, the August 28 hearing before Judge Walrath may sharpen to a narrower dispute over the sufficiency of document production rather than the full scope of Dkt. 73. That would be a partial win for Skillz — it secures the deposition — but would leave unresolved how much of the underlying documentary record Skillz can build before the recognition hearing.

For recovery analysis, nothing has shifted structurally. 
Judge Cote ordered Papaya to pay approximately $719 million in disgorgement, as well as approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and legal costs
 — that judgment remains stayed as to U.S. assets under Judge Walrath's temporary injunction. 
Papaya applied to the Tel Aviv District Court for a temporary stay, under which the company's available cash and current profits would be transferred to a designated fund held by an authorized representative on behalf of the court, intended to safeguard creditors' rights if Papaya's appeal is ultimately rejected.
 The adequacy of that fund — and Skillz's ability to contest recognition — still turns on how much of a factual record Skillz can assemble. Dkt. 77 represents one data point in that build. The next two hard deadlines are Papaya's written objection to Dkt. 73 on August 26 and the virtual discovery hearing before Judge Walrath on August 28, where the court will rule on the scope and timing of any compelled production.

On August 24, Poolin's professionals filed a retention application (Dkt. 179) and the first monthly fee statement in the case (Dkt. 178). The retention application is labeled "Do Not Use to Employ/Appoint an Examiner," indicating it concerns a professional other than an examiner — most likely a financial advisor, special counsel, or other estate professional. The fee statement is the first submitted under whatever interim compensation procedures the court has established. Neither filing is contested on the face of the docket; both are substantive but routine at this stage of a Chapter 11 wind-down. Two additional pro hac vice admissions (Dkts. 176–177) and eight BNC certificates (Dkts. 164–171) are procedural-and-routine and carry no independent weight.

One material piece of scheduling context not previously flagged in these briefings: 
the creditor's motion to appoint a Chapter 11 trustee (Dkt. 103) is set for hearing on October 21, 2026
, per case-tracking data from __[Elevenflo](https://elevenflo.com/cases/17582)__. That date matters for recovery posture. The trustee fight will not resolve before the September sale closes — meaning current management remains in control through the auction regardless of the motion's ultimate outcome. The trustee motion thus functions as a post-sale governance risk rather than a pre-sale disruption, unless the creditor moves to expedite, which there is no indication it has done.

The next two concrete milestones arrive in rapid succession: the nonbinding indications of interest deadline is Thursday, August 27, followed by the Section 341 creditors' meeting on August 28 at 9 a.m. ET (remote). 
Creditors are scheduled to meet remotely on August 28 at 9 a.m. ET for a Section 341 meeting, where creditors can question company representatives under oath.
 That examination is the first formal opportunity for the creditor body — including the ~11,700 wallet IOU holders — to question CRO Michael DuFrayne on the pre-petition fund movements underpinning Dkt. 103. The qualified bid deadline follows on September 8, and the auction on September 10, assuming at least one competing bid clears the qualification threshold; 
a sale hearing is set for September 18.

items.body_md:
On August 24, Judge Eumi K. Lee issued a cluster of orders in *In re Google Generative AI Copyright Litigation*, 5:23-cv-03440, resolving every major pending motion from the February 20 class certification hearing in a single day's docket activity. The central order is Dkt. 482 — an omnibus ruling that adjudicates the motion to certify the plaintiff class, Google's motion for sanctions, three motions for miscellaneous relief, an administrative motion under Civil Local Rule 7-11, and the outstanding motion to intervene. In a separate order (Dkt. 481), Judge Lee denied Dkt. 328, the Motion for Relief. Dkt. 480 granted Dkt. 269, Google's motion for leave to file supplemental authority — a routine procedural authorization that takes no classification above procedural-and-routine. Dkt. 479 resolved a sealing administrative motion, also procedural.

The operative question for recovery posture is the disposition in Dkt. 482 of the class certification motion. The docket entry confirms the order exists and that it resolves the certification motion, but does not recite the ruling's outcome in its text as reproduced here. What is confirmed: 
Judge Lee did not rule from the bench at the February 20 hearing on any of the motions to certify class, for sanctions, relief, or to intervene
 — meaning all four tracks were held under submission until this omnibus order. The sanctions motion is the one Google filed in November 2025, in which 
Google argued that plaintiffs had tried to "smuggle" in new classes into the lawsuit by seeking to certify multiple classes and subclasses of works "downloaded and/or ingested to develop" Google's generative AI models, whether used for training or not.
 Whether Judge Lee granted or denied sanctions — and whether she certified any class, a narrowed class, or none — are facts determinable only from the face of Dkt. 482 itself, which has not yet been reproduced in any secondary source confirmed in this cycle. The docket record is authoritative; the disposition is unverified and therefore not stated here.

What the chronology does establish is that this day's output concludes a phase of the case that has been under submission since February 20, approximately six months. The motion to certify class is substantive and dispositive of the plaintiff class's universe — certification defines who can share in any recovery and anchors the damages exposure Google faces on a per-work statutory-damages theory. 
Google's sanctions theory — that plaintiffs repositioned the case away from AI training by proposing classes defined around works "downloaded and/or ingested," not just trained-on — was briefed through February 5, 2026, with the hearing held February 20.
 Denial of the sanctions motion keeps plaintiffs' proposed class structure in play; a grant would have disciplinary and potentially structural consequences for class scope. The parallel denial of Dkt. 328 (Motion for Relief) closes a discrete contested track whose precise subject matter is not further described in the available docket text. On the intervention axis, Dkt. 482 also resolves the separate motion to intervene that remained pending after Cengage and Hachette withdrew their own intervention bid (Dkt. 342, resolved by Dkt. 477 on August 21) — the Lee Child/Andrew Child/Girlcomix motion filed at Dkt. 468 by consolidated plaintiffs, which had a hearing date set for February 20. The full text of Dkt. 482 — available on PACER at 5:23-cv-03440 — is the next document to pull; it will determine the class's shape, the sanctions outcome, and the case trajectory from here.

items.body_md:
On August 21, the clerk docketed Dkt. 684 — a USCA Case Number entry — confirming that the Ninth Circuit has accepted and assigned a docket number to at least one of the two pending fee appeals. The entry follows the notices filed by Edelson PC and Oppenheim + Zebrak (Dkt. 682, August 18) and Cowan DeBaets Abrahams & Sheppard LLP (Dkt. 683, August 19). The district court's notation of a USCA case number is the ministerial step that closes the opening of an appellate proceeding: the Ninth Circuit clerk has received the record, opened a case file, and issued a number that all subsequent appellate filings must reference. Whether the court assigned a single number to both appeals or opened two separate proceedings — and whether it has already or will sua sponte consolidate them — is not apparent from the face of Dkt. 684 alone and cannot be confirmed from available public sources this morning. The specific Ninth Circuit docket number(s) will become confirmable once the appellate docket appears on PACER or a public aggregator.

The substantive posture is unchanged but the procedural clock is now running at the appellate level. Once the Ninth Circuit issues its scheduling order — standard practice shortly after a case number is assigned — opening-brief deadlines will be set, typically running 40 days from the date the record on appeal is filed. 
The fee dispute at the core of both appeals centers on the district court's denial of class counsel's requested 12.5% fee (which would have yielded $187,500,000) and its substitution of a lodestar-multiplier award of $101,561,111 plus approximately $3 million in expense reimbursements
 — and, critically for the appellants, the exclusion of Edelson, Oppenheim + Zebrak, and Cowan DeBaets from any share of that award. Until opening briefs are filed, the precise legal theory each appellant group is pressing — fee exclusion only, or a broader challenge to the July 20 final approval order — remains unconfirmed on the face of the notices.

For class members, the assignment of a USCA case number is procedurally expected but consequential: it confirms the appellate track is live and the Effective Date has not arrived. The disbursement portal remains dormant, and the approximately 70% first-stage distribution stays in abeyance for the duration of the Ninth Circuit proceedings absent a court order or negotiated arrangement permitting earlier release of undisputed settlement funds. Anthropic's payment obligations run independently. 
The 30-day window from July 20 during which appeals could be noticed has now closed
, meaning the appellate record is set and no additional notices of appeal are expected. Anthropic's $450 million first installment (Scheduled Payment 1) falls due September 25, 2026 — that obligation is not stayed by the pending appeals, and no party has moved for a stay. The next concrete milestone is the Ninth Circuit's issuance of scheduling orders establishing opening-brief deadlines and formally resolving whether the two appeals proceed separately or on a consolidated track.

items.body_md:
On August 21, the Omnis Pleasants docket recorded a second wave of subpoenas — Dkts. 145 through 148 and 152 through 158, twelve in total — alongside two Chapter 11 first-day motion filings (Dkts. 142 and 144), a motion to file under seal (Dkt. 143), and a notice of service (Dkt. 159). The first-day motion filings at this stage of the case are not new petitions; they are almost certainly supplemental or amended first-day motions, or motions seeking approval of additional operational relief, filed as the debtor prepares for the September 3 final hearing complex. The motion to file under seal (Dkt. 143) is substantive to the extent its underlying subject matter is substantive — which, given the timing and context, likely involves materials bearing on the dismissal motion or the cash collateral record — but the sealing request itself does not independently move the case.

The twelve new subpoenas are the more consequential development. Combined with the fifteen subpoenas filed on August 20 (Dkts. 118–132, covered in Friday's briefing), the docket now reflects twenty-seven third-party subpoenas issued in a two-day window. That volume, compressed into 48 hours immediately before the August 28 objection deadline on the dismissal and trustee motion (Dkt. 93), is consistent with one or both sides conducting an accelerated pre-hearing discovery sweep keyed to the September 3 evidentiary proceedings. 
The August 14 motion filed by Omnis Fuel Technologies, LLC and Quantum Pleasants, LLC asks the court — if it declines dismissal — to appoint an independent Chapter 11 trustee and to vacate the interim cash collateral order.
 Third-party subpoenas at this stage would logically target witnesses with knowledge of the corporate authorization of the bankruptcy filing, the governance events of late July, and the circumstances surrounding the rejected $75.64 million payoff. The return dates on the subpoenas are not visible on the docket face but are presumably calibrated to produce documents and testimony before September 3.


The debtor is operating under interim cash-collateral authority while pursuing a sale of substantially all assets, with final approval set for September 3; the interim order (Dkt. 50) permits use of prepetition collateral under an approved budget, grants TRAG LLC and RG Energy LLC adequate protection, requires the debtor to continue the sale process, and limits any plan absent secured-party consent to one that pays those obligations in full in cash.
 That framework is directly in the crosshairs: a successful dismissal motion ends the case; a trustee appointment restructures who controls the sale. For unsecured creditors — including the West Virginia Economic Development Authority, 
Omnis Pleasants' largest creditor at more than $50.8 million, listed as unsecured
 — the outcome of the September 3 hearing complex is the central recovery variable. The debtor's Young Conaway and Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer teams are now simultaneously managing objections to a subpoena barrage, briefing the dismissal opposition due August 28, and preparing final-hearing submissions on wages, utilities, critical vendor payments, and cash collateral — all converging on a single hearing date. The next concrete milestone is August 28, the objection deadline on the dismissal and trustee motion (Dkt. 93), which will be the first substantive public indicator of the debtor's legal theory for why the case should survive.

items.body_md:
On August 21, Serrur Investment Partners, LP filed a transfer of claim (Dkt. 1323) in Case No. 24-10070-BLS, Bankr. D. Del., assigning a Class 5 Crypto Loss Claim with a face amount of $3,454,036.42 — the same transferee that filed three prior claim transfers on August 3 (Dkts. 1309–1311) and a Rule 3001(e)(2) notice of transfer for the same claim pool (Dkt. 1312). Dkt. 1323 is a substantive docket event in that it records a change in claim ownership, but it is routine at this stage: it does not alter the aggregate size of the Class 5 pool, the allowance status of the transferred claim, or any recovery percentage. It does confirm that secondary-market buying in Terraform's Crypto Loss Claim pool remains active heading into the fall, with Serrur accumulating at least five discrete transfers since early August. The identity of the transferor is withheld per the notice procedure used in Dkt. 1312, which stated that Serrur holds a signed Evidence of Transfer and will produce it to the Court, the debtors' claims agent, or relevant professionals on written request. Dkt. 1322 is a certificate of mailing and carries no independent significance.

The more consequential open item from the weekend concerns the SEC's Tai Mo Shan Fair Fund. 
The SEC faced an August 20 deadline to submit a plan for distributing the $123.1 million fund paid by Jump Crypto subsidiary Tai Mo Shan to investors harmed by Terra's 2022 collapse.
 
When the SEC extended the deadline in February, it said its staff needed additional time to develop the distribution methodology and, where appropriate, coordinate with anticipated distributions from the Terraform litigation.
 
Coordination with Terraform's separate bankruptcy recovery remains unresolved, and claims in the bankruptcy proceeding do not automatically establish eligibility for this fund.
 No SEC filing confirming submission of the distribution plan has surfaced as of this briefing; confirmation would take the form of a public SEC order or staff submission appearing on the SEC's EDGAR or enforcement docket. The Fair Fund is a parallel recovery track, not a bankruptcy estate asset, but its methodology — particularly how it defines eligible losses and coordinates with plan distributions — will directly affect the net recovery position of Class 5 claimants holding overlapping losses in both processes.

The authorization motion filed August 19 (Dkt. 1321), covered in the prior briefing, remains unresolved on the public record; no order granting or denying it has appeared on the docket. The next fixed milestone remains December 31, 2026 — the court-extended wind-down deadline — with the Jump Trading litigation and the *Chang v. Terraform Labs Wind Down Trust* adversary proceeding the primary near-term resolution triggers ahead of that date. Any SEC submission on the Tai Mo Shan Fair Fund distribution plan, if it landed on or around August 20, would be the most immediately actionable development for claimants to track this week.

items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.
